paragraphs: Let me now, as if from a height, look out over the world stripped of all its false and deceptive charms. The clear air lets me see each object as it truly is, while my heart is still. I am as calm as the landscape on a morning when the mists, slowly lifting, silently reveal the beauties of nature, refreshed by rest.
How will the world look now? I rub my eyes and wonder whether, perhaps, I am only just waking from a vivid dream.

I see the sons and daughters of men chasing shadows, and anxiously squandering their powers to feed passions that have no adequate object — were it not that the very excess of these blind impulses, pampered by that lying yet ever-trusted guide, the imagination, prepares them for some other state and so makes short-sighted mortals wiser without their own consent; or, what amounts to the same thing, while they were pursuing some imaginary present good.

After looking at things in this light, it would not be too fanciful to imagine that this world is a stage on which a pantomime is performed every day for the entertainment of superior beings. How amused they would be to watch the ambitious man wearing himself out in the chase after a phantom, pursuing the bubble fame into “the cannon’s mouth” that was to blow him to nothing: for once consciousness is gone, it makes no difference whether we rise in a whirlwind or fall as rain. And if they took pity on him and sharpened his sight, and showed him the thorny path that led to eminence — a path that sinks like quicksand as he climbs, cheating his hopes just when they are almost within his grasp — would he not leave to others the honour of amusing them, and strive to make sure of the present moment, even though the constitution of his nature would make it far from easy to catch the flying stream? Such slaves are we to hope and fear!

But, futile as the ambitious man’s pursuit would be, he is often striving for something more substantial than fame — which would indeed be the most fleeting of meteors, the wildest will-o’-the-wisp that ever lured a man to ruin. What! give up the smallest gratification in order to be applauded after he is gone! Why this struggle, whether man is mortal or immortal, if that noble passion did not truly raise the being above his fellows?

And love! What comic scenes it would provide — Pantaloon’s tricks would have to give way to more outrageous folly. To watch a mortal deck out an object with imaginary charms, and then fall down and worship the idol he himself had set up — how ridiculous! But what serious consequences follow, robbing man of that share of happiness which the Deity, in calling him into existence, has undoubtedly promised him (or else on what can his attributes rest?); would not all the purposes of life have been far better served if he had felt only what has been called physical love? And would not the sight of the object, when not seen through the medium of the imagination, soon reduce the passion to an appetite — if reflection, man’s noble distinction, did not give it force and make it a means of raising him above this earthly dross, by teaching him to love the centre of all perfection! whose wisdom shows more and more clearly in the works of nature as reason is enlightened and exalted by contemplation, and by gaining that love of order which the struggles of passion produce?

It could be shown that the habit of reflection, and the knowledge gained by nurturing any passion, are equally useful, even though the object proves equally illusory; for all objects would look alike if they were not magnified by the ruling passion which the Author of all good has planted in us, in order to call out and strengthen the faculties of each individual, and to let it gain all the experience that an infant can gain who does certain things without knowing why.

I come down from my height and, mingling with my fellow creatures, feel myself swept along by the common current; ambition, love, hope and fear exert their usual power, even though reason convinces us that their present and most attractive promises are only lying dreams. But if the cold hand of caution had damped each generous feeling before it had left any lasting mark on the character, or formed some habit, what could we expect but selfish prudence, and a reason barely rising above instinct? Who that has read with a philosophical eye Dean Swift’s disgusting description of the Yahoos, and his insipid one of the Houyhnhnm, can fail to see how futile it is to degrade the passions, or to make man rest content?

The young man should ACT; for if he had the experience of a grey head, he would be fitter for death than for life. His virtues, living in his head rather than his heart, could produce nothing great, and his understanding, trained for this world, would not show by any noble flights that it had a claim to a better one.

Besides, it is impossible to give a young person a true view of life; he must have wrestled with his own passions before he can gauge the strength of the temptation that led his brother into vice. Those who are setting out in life and those who are leaving it look at the world from such very different standpoints that they can rarely think alike — unless the unfledged reason of the young has never attempted a flight of its own.

When we hear of some daring crime, it strikes us full on, in the deepest shade of wickedness, and stirs our indignation; but the eye that watched the darkness gradually deepen must regard it with more compassionate forbearance. No unmoved spectator can see the world; we must mix in the crowd and feel as men feel before we can judge their feelings. In short, if we mean to live in the world so as to grow wiser and better, and not merely to enjoy life’s good things, we must come to know others at the same time as we come to know ourselves — knowledge gained in any other way only hardens the heart and confuses the understanding.

I may be told that knowledge gained in this way is sometimes bought too dearly. I can only reply that I very much doubt whether any knowledge can be acquired without labour and sorrow; and those who want to spare their children both should not complain if their children turn out neither wise nor virtuous. Their only aim was to make them prudent; and prudence, early in life, is nothing more than the wary craft of ignorant self-love. I have noticed that young people whose education received special attention have generally been very shallow and conceited, and not at all pleasing in any respect, because they had neither the trusting warmth of youth nor the cool depth of age. I cannot help blaming this unnatural character chiefly on that hasty, premature instruction which leads them to parrot, presumptuously, all the crude notions they have taken on trust; so that the careful education they received makes them lifelong slaves to prejudice.

Mental exertion, like physical exertion, is irksome at first — so much so that most people would gladly let others do both their working and their thinking for them. An observation I have often made will make my meaning clear. When, in a gathering of strangers or acquaintances, a person of moderate abilities asserts an opinion heatedly, I will venture to say — for I have very often traced the fact to its source — that it is a prejudice. These echoes hold the understanding of some relative or friend in high regard, and, without fully grasping the opinions they are so eager to peddle, they defend them with a stubbornness that would astonish even the person who first devised them.

I know that a certain fashion for respecting prejudices now prevails; and when anyone dares to confront them, though moved by humanity and armed with reason, he is asked with disdain whether his ancestors were fools. No, I would answer; opinions of every kind were probably all considered at first, and were therefore founded on some reason; yet, naturally enough, that reason was quite often a local expedient rather than a fundamental principle that would hold good at all times. But moss-covered opinions take on the misshapen form of prejudices when they are lazily adopted merely because age has given them a venerable look, even though the reason on which they were built has ceased to be a reason, or can no longer be traced. Why should we love prejudices simply because they are prejudices? A prejudice is a doting, obstinate conviction for which we can give no reason; for the moment a reason can be given for an opinion, it stops being a prejudice, though it may still be an error of judgment. Are we then advised to cherish opinions only in order to defy reason? This way of arguing, if it deserves to be called arguing, reminds me of what is commonly called a woman’s reason. For women sometimes declare that they love or believe certain things BECAUSE they love or believe them.

It is impossible to have a useful conversation with people who, in this manner, only ever say yes or no. Before you can bring them to a point from which you can fairly begin, you have to go back to the simple principles that existed before power spread its prejudices abroad; and it is ten to one that you will be halted by the philosophical claim that certain principles are as false in practice as they are true in the abstract. Indeed, one may infer that reason has whispered some doubts; for people generally assert their opinions most heatedly just when they begin to waver: trying to drive out their own doubts by convincing their opponent, they grow angry when those gnawing doubts are flung back to prey upon them.

The truth is that men expect from education what education cannot give. A wise parent or tutor can strengthen the body and sharpen the tools with which the child is to gather knowledge; but the honey must be the reward of the individual’s own industry. It is almost as absurd to try to make a youth wise through another person’s experience as to expect the body to grow strong through exercise that is only talked about or watched.

Many of the children whose conduct has been most closely watched grow into the weakest men, because their instructors merely instil certain notions into their minds that rest on nothing but the instructors’ authority; and if the children love or respect them, the mind is cramped in its efforts and hesitant in its progress. In this case the business of education is only to guide the shooting tendrils to a proper pole; yet after heaping precept upon precept, without letting a child form any judgment of its own, parents expect their children to act by this borrowed, deceptive light just as if they had kindled it themselves, and to be, when they enter life, what their parents are at its close. They forget that a tree, and even the human body, does not strengthen its fibres until it has reached its full growth.

Something similar seems to hold for the mind. During childhood and youth, the senses and the imagination shape the character; and as life goes on, the understanding lends firmness to the first fair intentions of sensibility — until, with virtue springing from the clear conviction of reason rather than from the impulse of the heart, morality comes to rest on a rock against which the storms of passion beat in vain.

I hope I shall not be misunderstood when I say that religion will not have this consolidating force unless it is grounded in reason. If it is merely a refuge for weakness or for wild fanaticism, and not a governing principle of conduct drawn from self-knowledge and a rational understanding of God’s attributes, what can we expect it to produce? The religion that consists in warming the feelings and exalting the imagination is only its poetic part, and may give the individual pleasure without making it a more moral being. It may replace worldly pursuits, yet narrow the heart rather than enlarge it: but virtue must be loved as sublime and excellent in itself, and not for the benefits it brings or the evils it wards off, if any high degree of excellence is to be expected. Men will not become moral while they merely build castles in the air in a future world to make up for the disappointments they meet in this one — if they turn their thoughts away from their duties to one another towards religious reveries.

Most prospects in life are spoiled by the shuffling worldly wisdom of men who, forgetting that they cannot serve God and mammon, try to combine things that contradict each other. If you want to make your son rich, take one course — if your only concern is to make him virtuous, you must take another; but do not imagine that you can jump from one road to the other without losing your way.*
(*Footnote. See an excellent essay on this subject by Mrs. Barbauld, in Miscellaneous pieces in Prose.)
